author: ribeye
dek: A Mentor couple's long-planned fall trip to ride the scenic railroad in north Georgia ran into 18 feet of river instead.
disclaimer: Parody: the Whitaker family of Mentor is fictional. The record Georgia flooding is real, as reported by the Associated Press in November 2026.
headline: Mentor Family's Blue Ridge Train Trip Gets Washed Out — Literally

ohio_quotes.quote: I checked the weather for Blue Ridge three times a day for a month. I never once thought to check the river.
ohio_quotes.speaker: Tom Whitaker, Mentor

ohio_quotes.quote: We were supposed to be sipping coffee on a train through the mountains. Instead we spent the morning watching a police car float down a river on the news, and I still can't get over that part.
ohio_quotes.speaker: Karen Whitaker, Mentor

ohio_story: MENTOR, Ohio — Tom and Karen Whitaker did everything right. They booked the cabin outside Blue Ridge, Georgia, months ago, printed the tickets for the Blue Ridge Scenic Railway, and even bought a new pair of binoculars for the fall colors, which Karen insists are "a whole different orange than Ohio orange." Their train was supposed to roll out of the depot Thursday morning. Instead, Thursday morning, the Toccoa River rolled through downtown McCaysville, about an hour from their cabin, at a record 18 feet.

Karen found out from the cabin owner, who called to say the road to the cabin was washed out, the train was not running, and would they please not drive down anyway, because half the town was currently floating. The Whitakers spent Thursday morning on the couch in Mentor watching rescue boats on the news, the packed car sitting in the driveway like a dog that had been promised a walk. Tom, who had checked the Blue Ridge weather three times a day for a month, kept refreshing the river gauge instead. "It went up a foot while I was making toast," he said. "I have never watched a river the way I watch the Browns."

The trip is now rescheduled for spring, when the Whitakers hope the only thing running high is the pollen count. As a consolation prize, they drove out to Headlands Beach State Park on Saturday and watched the Lake Erie waves come in. "The closest thing to a scenic railroad in November is standing at Headlands pretending the wind is a train whistle," Tom said. Karen has already started a new packing list. The binoculars, she notes, are staying in the bag this time — "just in case the river decides to follow us home."
real_summary: Thunderstorms caused record flooding overnight in the twin towns straddling the Georgia-Tennessee border, submerging some buildings to their rooflines on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, as emergency responders rescued dozens of people in McCaysville, Georgia, and Copperhill, Tennessee.

As much as 8 to 10 inches of rain fell overnight between the north Georgia towns of Blue Ridge and Ellijay, and runoff swelled the Toccoa River, which reached a record high Thursday morning of 18 feet at a river gauge in Copperhill, 2 feet above the level forecasters consider catastrophic. McCaysville Police Chief Michael Earley said the water flowed over rooftops in some places and reached about 6 to 7 feet high in the small downtown.

At least 57 people were rescued by swift-water teams, according to the Fannin County Emergency Management Agency in Georgia, and the Tennessee Emergency Management Authority said it had coordinated 68 rescues by swift-water teams. The flooding shut down the McCaysville water treatment plant, prompting a boil-water advisory, and was complicated by cellphone and power outages. One firefighter suffered a minor injury and a few residents were treated for suspected hypothermia and shock. The towns had also been hit by another damaging flood in August.
source_note: AP reporting, Nov 2026: record flooding in McCaysville, Georgia, and Copperhill, Tennessee, after overnight storms dropped 8 to 10 inches of rain.
